title: C Standard Library
relevance: Interviews and OAs test whether candidates treat libc as a thin OS-backed layer and choose safe I/O, string, and conversion APIs instead of overflow-prone or silent-failure defaults.

phases.goal: Establish that C itself is tiny and that libc availability depends on hosted vs freestanding execution environments.

must_hit.point: The C language provides almost no built-in primitives for I/O, memory allocation, or string manipulation; those come from the C Standard Library (libc).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate separates language from libc and names I/O, malloc-family, and string ops as library, not language, features.

must_hit.point: A hosted environment (Linux, Windows, macOS) supplies a full standard library and program entry at main; a freestanding environment (embedded firmware, OS kernels) does not provide a file system or dynamic memory by default.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts fully furnished hosted libc with freestanding limits and gives an embedded or kernel example.

must_hit.point: Freestanding guarantees only a few essential headers such as stdint.h, stddef.h, stdbool.h, limits.h, and float.h; OS-dependent headers like stdio.h and stdlib.h are absent.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate lists type/limit headers as freestanding and excludes stdio/stdlib as requiring an OS.

probes: What is the difference between a hosted and a freestanding C environment, and which headers can you still rely on without an OS?

hints.1: Think about where printf text would go on a bare-metal microcontroller with no screen or OS.
hints.2: Hosted starts at main with full libc; freestanding keeps only limits and type headers.
hints.3: Freestanding includes stdint/stddef/stdbool/limits/float; stdio and stdlib are not guaranteed.

phases.goal: Check precise mechanics of streams, bounded formatting, robust conversion, memory copy rules, and error/assert plumbing.

must_hit.point: In a hosted program, three text streams open automatically: stdin, stdout, and stderr; disk files are handled via an opaque FILE* that holds stream state including position and error flags.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names the three standard streams and describes FILE* as opaque stream state, not a user-visible struct layout.

must_hit.point: Most I/O is buffered and flushed when the buffer fills, on fclose, or via fflush; stderr is unbuffered by default so errors appear immediately if the program crashes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains buffer-then-flush behavior and specially calls out unbuffered stderr.

must_hit.point: snprintf writes at most size - 1 characters into the destination and always appends a null terminator; its return value is how many characters would have been written if the buffer were large enough, which detects truncation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate cites the size - 1 write limit, guaranteed '\0', and truncation detection via the return value.

must_hit.point: strtol parses with an endptr and base; on range errors it returns LONG_MAX or LONG_MIN and sets errno to ERANGE, unlike atoi which cannot distinguish valid "0" from invalid input and can invoke undefined behavior on overflow.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts silent atoi with strtol's endptr plus ERANGE/LONG_MAX/LONG_MIN handling.

must_hit.point: memcpy assumes disjoint regions (restrict enables optimization) and yields undefined behavior on overlap; memmove is safe for overlapping source and destination.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate ties restrict/non-overlap to memcpy speed and names memmove for overlapping copies.

must_hit.point: Library failures often return a sentinel (NULL or -1) and set thread-local errno; assert is for impossible programmer logic errors and is compiled out entirely when NDEBUG is defined.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate pairs sentinel returns with errno/perror/strerror and states asserts vanish under NDEBUG.

probes: How does snprintf prevent buffer overflow, and what does its return value tell you?
Walk through checking a strtol conversion for overflow, no digits, and trailing garbage.

hints.1: Compare writing into a fixed char array with sprintf versus snprintf.
hints.2: For snprintf, reason about size - 1 and the null terminator; for strtol, reason about errno, endptr == input, and *endptr.
hints.3: snprintf caps at size - 1 and null-terminates; after strtol, ERANGE means out of range, endptr == input means no conversion, and *endptr == '\0' means the whole string was numeric.

phases.goal: Surface when safer libc choices beat convenient but fragile defaults in I/O, conversion, copying, and embedded constraints.

must_hit.point: Prefer fgets over scanf for line input: scanf can leave invalid tokens in the stream and loop forever, while fgets reads a bounded line then you parse the buffer.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes leftover input after a failed scanf("%d") and the fgets-then-parse pattern.

must_hit.point: In embedded firmware, avoid malloc for non-deterministic latency and heap fragmentation on long-running systems, and avoid printf because it is bloated in scarce ROM; prefer static allocation and lightweight custom formatting.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names timing/fragmentation for malloc and ROM cost for printf even when a vendor libc exists.

must_hit.point: Use memcpy for non-overlapping block copies for speed; switch to memmove when regions may overlap.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate picks memcpy when disjoint and memmove when overlap is possible, without claiming memcpy is always safe.

probes: Why prefer fgets over scanf when reading user lines?
Even with a vendor libc, why might embedded code still avoid malloc and printf?

hints.1: Consider what remains in stdin after a user types letters where a number was expected.
hints.2: Separate interactive parsing robustness from heap/ROM constraints on microcontrollers.
hints.3: fgets bounds the line then you parse; malloc adds fragmentation and jitter, printf costs ROM, so firmware often uses static buffers and tiny formatters.

phases.goal: Apply safe libc patterns for file reading, integer parsing, formatting, and user-controlled output.

must_hit.point: Safe file reading pairs fopen with error checks via NULL/perror, loops with fgets into a fixed buffer, optionally strips a trailing newline, and always fclose before EXIT_SUCCESS or EXIT_FAILURE.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate sketches fopen check, fgets loop, newline strip via strlen, fclose, and standard exit statuses.

must_hit.point: Robust integer parsing resets errno to 0, calls strtol with base 10, then branches on ERANGE, endptr == input (no digits), and otherwise inspects *endptr for trailing characters.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate orders errno=0, strtol, ERANGE check, no-conversion check, then trailing-character notice.

must_hit.point: Never pass raw user input as a printf format string; use printf("%s", user_input) so %s/%n in the input cannot read or write arbitrary stack memory.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate rejects printf(user_input) and insists on a literal "%s" format with the string as an argument.

probes: Write the checks you would run after strtol to accept only a pure integer string.
How do you safely print a string that came from the user?

hints.1: Remember library calls do not clear errno on success, so set it before strtol.
hints.2: Check range via errno, then whether endptr advanced, then whether *endptr is the null terminator.
hints.3: errno=0; strtol(..., &endptr, 10); fail on ERANGE or endptr==input; require *endptr=='\0' for a pure number; print users with printf("%s", ...).

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Hosted environments give full libc and main; freestanding (firmware/kernels) only guarantee essential type/limit headers, so PC programs that call stdio/stdlib must be stripped or rewritten before porting to bare metal.

tradeoffs.topic: fgets vs scanf for line input
tradeoffs.strong_answer: fgets bounds the read into a buffer you then parse; scanf formatted reads are fragile because a mismatch leaves bad tokens in the stream and can cause infinite retry loops.

sprintf can overflow the destination with no size check; snprintf takes the buffer size, writes at most size - 1 chars, null-terminates, and returns the would-be length so truncation is detectable—unless you pass the wrong size such as sizeof on a char* (often 8).
atoi cannot tell valid "0" from garbage and overflows with undefined behavior; strtol exposes endptr for leftover text and sets errno to ERANGE with LONG_MAX/LONG_MIN on range errors.
memcpy is the fast disjoint copy and its restrict contract enables optimization, but overlapping regions are undefined; memmove is correct when source and destination may overlap.

tradeoffs.topic: malloc/printf vs static/custom I/O in embedded
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Even with a minimal vendor libc, malloc brings non-deterministic time and fragmentation risk on systems that cannot reboot, and printf consumes scarce ROM, so firmware often uses static allocation and lightweight formatters.

gotchas.trap: Using gets(buffer) from older books for line input.
gotchas.correction: gets was removed in C11 because it has no size parameter and will overflow the buffer on a long line; never use it.

gotchas.trap: Calling printf(user_input) with untrusted text as the format string.
gotchas.correction: If the input contains %s or %n, printf treats them as format directives; always use printf("%s", user_input).

gotchas.trap: Treating strncpy(dest, src, n) as a strictly safer strcpy.
gotchas.correction: If src is longer than n, strncpy does not append a null terminator; prefer snprintf(dest, n, "%s", src) or POSIX strlcpy.

gotchas.trap: Passing a signed char into ctype.h predicates like isdigit.
gotchas.correction: Those APIs take int so they can accept EOF (usually -1); cast char values to unsigned char first or negative non-EOF values are undefined behavior.
Unclosed files leak OS file-table slots and may lose buffered output that never gets flushed.

gotchas.trap: Using strtok across threads or recursively.
gotchas.correction: strtok mutates the input and keeps hidden static parse state, so it is not thread-safe and cannot be nested.
rand is deterministic once seeded and cryptographically weak; seed with srand only for non-security uses.

gotchas.trap: Relying on assert for expected runtime failures, or forgetting NDEBUG.
gotchas.correction: assert is for impossible programmer logic bugs; with NDEBUG defined, asserts are removed and cost zero CPU in production.
